title: You Read Your New Team Wrong
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions (theartofaskingquestions.com), September 27, 2026
summary: Chiarelli tells the story of Giulia Scalaberni, a product lead whose onboarding calls with a newly assigned team in India ended in silence every time she asked for questions. Her first explanations, shyness, language barriers or full comprehension, all blamed the individuals rather than the meeting she designed. The silence did not thin out over time, which pushed her to test a different hypothesis drawn from Erin Meyer's Culture Map and Hofstede's dimensions. Her task-based, agenda-driven meeting format clashed with a relationship-based trust default on the other side. A two-hour session built around names, roles and hobbies produced immediate openness, and the same 'any questions?' prompt finally got answers. Chiarelli's broader lesson is that a leader's first read of a situation should be treated as a working hypothesis that can be wrong.
points: Repeated silence that does not fade with time is evidence that the cause is structural, not personal shyness or language.
Meeting formats embed a theory of trust; an agenda-and-execution format assumes trust is earned by delivering, which a relationship-first team will not share.
A small, low-cost test, such as a session of introductions and shared interests, can confirm or overturn a cultural diagnosis within a week.
Cultural lenses such as Meyer's scales explain friction (lateness, directness, silence) that is otherwise filed under individual quirks, and the fix is adjusting expectations, not policing behavior.
The fixes themselves do not transfer between teams; what transfers is the habit of treating your first explanation as a hypothesis.
quotes: If the causes for limited engagement from her remote team had been shyness or comprehension gaps in either direction, the silence should have thinned out over time. But that didn’t change, and this is what led Giulia to realising that her first read was wrong.

One of Meyer’s central ideas is cultural relativity: the same culture can be read in opposite ways depending on who’s judging it. Italians can legitimately look chaotic to UK colleagues and too rigid to Indian ones.
A sharp agenda and a round of introductions followed by an hour of execution detail is closer to a task-based trust design. Confidence is earned by delivering, not by getting to know someone.
So she got an updated understanding of what was happening: the silence was a structural mismatch between how her meeting extended trust and what her team needed.
The change was immediate. Person after person, including the members of the team she’d identified as the most quiet, found some shared ground, from tennis, to cricket, to children.
A colleague who was always late was the clearest case. They would agree to meet in a hotel lobby at 6pm, which reliably meant a start closer to 6.20pm.
The one thing that you can apply right away to your own practice is the habit of never accepting the first explanation you see just because it’s quick to arrive and ‘feels obvious’.
That is a real leadership skill: it’s the ability to treat your own read of a situation as a working hypothesis - and always being open to being found wrong.
